title: Hook
text: Can the way you position your arms and legs actually change how you fall from the sky? Skydivers say yes.
nxt: And the worst thing you can do is curl into a tight ball.

title: Gravity and Drag
text: When you fall, gravity pulls you down and the air pushes back. That push is aerodynamic drag, and it grows as you speed up.
nxt: Soon the two forces balance, your acceleration stops, and you reach terminal velocity.

title: The Ball
text: Curling up shrinks your surface area. With less body in the way of the rushing air, you slice through it, and your falling speed rises.
nxt: If your goal is to slow down, the ball is a poor choice.

title: Spread-Eagle
text: Skydivers use the belly-to-earth spread-eagle. Arms and legs go wide, your back arches slightly, and your chest faces the ground.
nxt: Now your body catches as many air molecules as possible,

title: Stability
text: Spreading out also keeps you stable.
nxt: An uneven object can fall into a violent flat spin, and a fast spin can cause dizziness and even blackouts.

nxt: Outstretched limbs act like the four fins of a rocket and damp the rotation. You can even steer a little by tilting your hands and shoulders.

title: Feet First
text: Then, in the final moments, the usual advice is a feet-first landing with slightly bent knees.
nxt: The long bones of the legs, the ankles, and the pelvis are among the sturdiest in the body.

title: The Roll
text: Military parachutists add one more trick, the parachute landing fall.
nxt: Boots touch down, then the body collapses to the side and rolls across the calf, thigh, hip, and back.

title: Honest Limit
text: None of this makes a fall from ten kilometers safe. A roll cannot cancel that much speed, and luck plays the dominant role.
nxt: But the ideas are the same ones again and again: spread the impact over more body and more time.
